documents.prompt: A {{vehicle}} uses {{g1}} gallons of fuel to travel {{m1}} miles. At that rate, how many gallons are needed to travel {{m2}} miles?

solutionReview.headline: Find what one gallon covers, then share the new distance into it.
reasoning: {{m1}} miles on {{g1}} gallons is {{mpg}} miles per gallon.

attemptFeedback: Check which distance goes with which amount of fuel.
supportHints: Work out how far the {{vehicle}} goes on a single gallon first.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} sells {{item}} at {{n1}} for $\${{p1}}$ or {{n2}} for $\${{p2}}$. At the lower price per item, what do {{need}} {{item}} cost?

solutionReview.headline: Compare per item, then buy at that price.

attemptFeedback: Decide which offer is cheaper per item, then use that price.
supportHints: Find what one item costs under each offer before deciding.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} of {{total}} people is split between loading and driving in a ratio of {{m}} to {{n}}. How many are loading?

solutionReview.headline: A ratio splits a total into equal shares.
reasoning: The ratio splits the {{crew}} into {{m}}+{{n}} equal shares.

attemptFeedback: The two numbers in the ratio count shares, not people.
supportHints: Work out how many equal shares the total is divided into.

documents.prompt: An order calls for {{needed}} {{item}}. A {{machine}} makes {{rate}} an hour and runs {{hours}} hours. How many {{item}} are still owed?

solutionReview.headline: Produce first, then compare against the order.
reasoning: In {{hours}} hours the {{machine}} makes {{rate}} times {{hours}}, or {{made}}.

attemptFeedback: The question asks what remains, not how many were produced.
supportHints: Work out how many were made before looking at what is left.

documents.prompt: A {{machine}} runs two stretches at the rates shown. How many {{item}} does it make in all?

solutionReview.headline: Each rate only applies to its own stretch of time.

attemptFeedback: Pair each hourly amount with the hours it actually ran.
supportHints: Each stretch of time has its own hourly amount. Handle them one at a time.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} has {{small}} {{item}} on the floor and {{big}} in the back. How many times as many are in the back?

solutionReview.headline: How many times as many is a division.
reasoning: Comparing two counts of the same thing is a division, not a subtraction.
solutionReview.answerSummary: There are ${{answer}}$ times as many in the back.

attemptFeedback: How many times as many is not the same as how many more.
supportHints: Ask how many floor-sized groups fit into the back stock.

documents.prompt: A batch has {{redCount}} {{first}} and {{blueCount}} {{second}}. In lowest terms, what is the ratio of {{first}} to {{second}}?

solutionReview.headline: Both counts divide by their common factor.

attemptFeedback: The order of the two numbers follows the order named in the question.
supportHints: Look for a number that divides both counts.

documents.prompt: In a {{crew}} the ratio of {{first}} to {{second}} is {{a}} to {{b}}. There are {{firstCount}} {{first}}. How many {{second}} are there?

solutionReview.headline: Both parts of a ratio scale by the same factor.

attemptFeedback: Both sides of the ratio grow by the same factor, not by the same amount.
supportHints: Work out how many times the ratio has been scaled up.

documents.prompt: A shipment holds {{first}} and {{second}} in a ratio of {{a}} to {{b}}. What fraction of the shipment is {{first}}?

solutionReview.headline: A part-to-part ratio becomes a part-to-whole fraction by adding the parts.
reasoning: The shipment is {{a}}+{{b}} equal parts, or {{whole}} in all.

attemptFeedback: The bottom of the fraction is the whole, not the other part.
supportHints: Count how many equal parts the whole shipment contains.

documents.prompt: The mix below must stay at a ratio of {{a}} to {{b}}. How many {{second}} go with {{firstCount}} {{first}}?

solutionReview.headline: An equivalent ratio multiplies both entries by the same number.
reasoning: The first row was multiplied by {{scale}} to reach {{firstCount}}.

attemptFeedback: Adding the same amount to both entries changes the ratio; multiplying keeps it.
supportHints: Compare the two rows in the first column.

documents.prompt: A {{vehicle}} covers {{miles}} miles on {{gal}} gallons. How many miles per gallon is that?

solutionReview.headline: A rate divides one quantity by the other.
reasoning: Miles per gallon shares the miles among the gallons.

attemptFeedback: Miles per gallon puts miles on top.
supportHints: Decide which quantity is being shared out and which does the sharing.

documents.prompt: A case of {{count}} {{item}} costs $\${{total}}$, and shipping adds $\${{ship}}$. What does one {{item}} cost delivered?

solutionReview.headline: Both charges have to come down to a single item before they add.
reasoning: The case works out to $\${{each}}$ an item.
Shipping adds $\${{ship}}$ over {{count}} items, or $\${{perItemShip}}$ each.

attemptFeedback: Bring the shipping down to a per-item amount before adding it on.
supportHints: Shipping covers the whole case, not one item.

documents.prompt: Two {{machine}}s ran the outputs shown. How many more {{item}} an hour does the faster one make?

solutionReview.headline: Two totals over different hours only compare per hour.
reasoning: Machine A runs at {{outA}} over {{hA}} hours, or {{fast}} an hour.
Machine B runs at {{slow}} an hour.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The faster one makes ${{answer}}$ more an hour.

attemptFeedback: Compare the hourly rates, not the totals.
supportHints: Neither total means anything until both are per hour.

documents.prompt: A {{machine}} fills {{rate}} {{item}} a minute. How many does it fill in {{mins}} minutes?

solutionReview.headline: A rate multiplied by the time gives the total.

attemptFeedback: A per-minute amount multiplies by the minutes; it does not add to them.
supportHints: One minute is worth the rate. Count the minutes.

documents.prompt: {{item}} sell at $\${{perDozen}}$ a dozen. At that rate, what do {{want}} {{item}} cost?

solutionReview.headline: Come down to one before going up to the amount asked.
reasoning: A dozen is 12, so one costs $\${{perDozen}}$ over 12, or $\${{each}}$.

attemptFeedback: The quoted price covers twelve, not one.
supportHints: Work out what a single one costs first.

documents.prompt: On a plan, {{inches}} inch stands for {{feet}} feet. A wall drawn {{drawn}} inches long is how many feet long?

solutionReview.headline: A scale converts each drawn unit into real units.
reasoning: Every drawn inch is {{feet}} real feet.

attemptFeedback: Each inch on the plan carries the same number of real feet.
supportHints: Decide what one drawn inch is worth in real life.

documents.prompt: A model is built at {{scale}} to 1. The real {{part}} is {{real}} centimetres. How many centimetres is it on the model?

solutionReview.headline: Going from real to model divides by the scale.
reasoning: The real {{part}} is {{scale}} times the model.
solutionReview.answerSummary: It is ${{answer}}$ centimetres on the model.

attemptFeedback: Scaling up and scaling down are opposite operations.
supportHints: The model is the smaller of the two. Which operation makes a number smaller?

documents.prompt: The table keeps a constant rate. What belongs in the empty cell?

solutionReview.headline: A constant rate multiplies, row by row.
reasoning: The first row pairs {{a1}} with {{b1}}, so each {{unitA}} is worth {{k}}.

attemptFeedback: The rows are linked by multiplying, not by adding the same amount.
supportHints: Work out what one unit in the left column is worth.

documents.prompt: A mix uses {{partA}} parts {{matA}} to {{partB}} parts {{matB}}. To use {{useA}} pounds of {{matA}}, how many pounds of {{matB}} are needed?

solutionReview.headline: Both ingredients scale by the same number of batches.

attemptFeedback: Both parts of the mix grow by the same factor.
supportHints: Count how many whole batches the given amount makes.

documents.prompt: {{count}} {{item}} cost $\${{total}}$. How many {{item}} can be bought with $\${{budget}}$?

solutionReview.headline: Get the price of one, then see how many the budget covers.

attemptFeedback: Divide the budget by the price of one, not by the number in the first offer.
supportHints: A budget question needs the price of a single item first.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} enters a {{p}}% fee into a register that takes decimals. Which decimal does it enter?

solutionReview.headline: Percent means per hundred.

attemptFeedback: Moving the point one place gives tenths, not hundredths.
supportHints: How many hundredths does the percent name?

documents.prompt: A 10 by 10 grid has {{shaded}} squares shaded. What percent of the grid is shaded?

stimulus.title: Grid record
stimulus.note: {{shaded}} of the 100 squares are shaded and {{unshaded}} are blank.

solutionReview.headline: A hundred-square grid reads straight off as a percent.
reasoning: The grid holds 100 squares, so each square is one percent.

attemptFeedback: The question asks about the shaded part, not the blank part.
supportHints: Count how many squares the whole grid holds.

documents.prompt: {{num}} out of every {{den}} {{item}} pass inspection. What percent pass?

solutionReview.headline: A percent is the same ratio rewritten out of 100.
reasoning: {{den}} goes into 100 a whole number of times.
Scaling {{num}} out of {{den}} up to hundredths gives {{answer}} out of 100.

attemptFeedback: The count that passes is not already a percent.
supportHints: Scale the comparison so the second number becomes 100.

documents.prompt: {{p}}% of a {{total}}-{{item}} order arrived early. How many arrived early?

solutionReview.headline: Find one percent, then take as many as the percent names.

attemptFeedback: The percent is a share of the order, not a count on its own.
supportHints: Work out what one percent of the order is.

documents.prompt: Four {{shop}} discounts are written in different forms. Which is the largest?

solutionReview.headline: Percents, fractions and decimals only compare in one shared form.
reasoning: Put every option in the same form first.
{{bigDec}} is {{big}}%, {{mid}}% is {{midDec}}, and the last two are {{lowDec}} and {{tenth}}.

attemptFeedback: A larger-looking number is not larger once the forms match.
supportHints: Rewrite each option the same way before comparing.

documents.prompt: A {{tool}} listed at $\${{total}}$ is marked down {{p}}%. How much is taken off?

solutionReview.headline: A markdown is a percent of the listed price.

attemptFeedback: The markdown is the part taken off, not the part left.
supportHints: Work out one percent of the listed price first.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} cleared {{p}}% of {{total}} {{item}} on the first day and {{q}}% of the total on the second. How many are left?

solutionReview.headline: Both percents are of the same total, so they add.
reasoning: Together the two days cleared {{p}}+{{q}} percent of the order.

attemptFeedback: Add the two shares before taking them off the total.
supportHints: Both days are measured against the original order.

documents.prompt: 1% of a shipment is {{one}} {{item}}. How many {{item}} are {{p}}% of it?

solutionReview.headline: One percent is the unit every other percent is built from.

attemptFeedback: The whole shipment is 100 percent; the question asks for less than that.
supportHints: One percent is a building block. How many of them does the question want?

documents.prompt: {{part}} {{item}} are {{num}} of the {{den}} equal shares of a load, and {{extra}} more were added. How many {{item}} are there now?

solutionReview.headline: Get to one share before rebuilding the whole.
reasoning: {{part}} covers {{num}} shares, so one share is {{share}}.
The whole load is {{den}} shares, or {{load}}.

attemptFeedback: The given count covers several shares, not one.
supportHints: Work out the size of a single share first.

documents.prompt: A strip of {{total}} {{item}} is split into the parts shown. What percent is {{label1}}?

solutionReview.headline: A part of a whole becomes a percent by comparing it to the whole.
reasoning: {{part1}} out of {{total}} is the share being asked for.
That is {{answer}} out of every hundred.

attemptFeedback: Read the row the question names, not the other one.
supportHints: Compare the part named in the question with the whole strip.

documents.prompt: A bill of $\${{bill}}$ is paid with a tip of $\${{tip}}$. What percent of the bill is the tip?

solutionReview.headline: A part becomes a percent by comparing it to the whole.
solutionReview.answerSummary: The tip is ${{answer}}\%$ of the bill.

attemptFeedback: Compare the tip with the bill, not with what is left over.
supportHints: Work out what one percent of the bill is worth.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} charges $\${{cents}}$ cents for each {{item}}. What do {{count}} {{item}} cost in dollars?

solutionReview.headline: Cents become dollars a hundred at a time.
reasoning: A hundred cents is a dollar, so that is {{answer}} dollars.

attemptFeedback: A hundred cents make a dollar.
supportHints: Total the cents first, then change to dollars.

documents.prompt: A {{tool}} costs $\${{price}}$. One {{shop}} takes {{p}}% off and another takes $\${{flat}}$ off. How much cheaper is the better offer?

solutionReview.headline: A percent off and an amount off only compare once both are amounts.

attemptFeedback: The question asks for the difference between the two savings.
supportHints: Turn the percent into an amount of money before comparing.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} rounds a price to {{num}} of {{den}} equal parts of a dollar. How many cents is that?

solutionReview.headline: A fraction of a dollar is that fraction of 100 cents.
reasoning: A dollar is 100 cents split into {{den}} parts.

attemptFeedback: Check which of the two numbers counts the parts.
supportHints: Split 100 cents into the number of parts named.

documents.prompt: A {{p}}% deposit on a {{tool}} comes to $\${{deposit}}$. What is the full price?

solutionReview.headline: Work back from the percent paid to the whole.
reasoning: One percent is {{hundreds}}, so the full hundred percent is {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: The deposit is part of the price, so the price is larger.
supportHints: Find what one percent of the price is worth.

documents.prompt: A {{part}} measures {{feet}} feet {{inches}} inches. How many inches is that in all?

solutionReview.headline: Only the feet need converting; the inches are already inches.
reasoning: The extra {{inches}} inches bring it to {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: Check which measurement counts feet and which counts inches.
supportHints: A foot is twelve inches.

documents.prompt: A crate holds {{ounces}} ounces of {{item}}. How many whole pounds is that?

solutionReview.headline: Sixteen ounces make a pound.
reasoning: {{ounces}} ounces holds {{answer}} whole pounds with {{spare}} ounces over.

attemptFeedback: Check how many ounces make one pound.
supportHints: How many groups of sixteen fit in the total?

documents.prompt: A tank takes {{quarts}} quarts to fill. A pump moves {{gpm}} gallons a minute. How many minutes does filling take?

solutionReview.headline: Match the units before using the rate.
reasoning: Four quarts make a gallon, so {{quarts}} quarts is {{gallons}} gallons.

attemptFeedback: Convert to the pump’s units before dividing.
supportHints: The tank is measured in quarts but the pump works in gallons.

documents.prompt: A job needs {{pieces}} pieces of {{part}}, each {{feetEach}} feet long, plus {{extra}} yards spare. Material is sold by the yard. How many yards are needed?

solutionReview.headline: Total in one unit, then convert once.
reasoning: {{pieces}} pieces at {{feetEach}} feet is {{totalFeet}} feet, or {{d_forgotFinalStep}} yards.

attemptFeedback: Three feet make a yard, so the yard count is smaller than the foot count.
supportHints: Add up all the material first, then change units.

documents.prompt: Using the table, how many {{small}} are in {{bigCount}} {{big}}?

solutionReview.headline: A conversion table gives the rate for one unit.

attemptFeedback: Converting to a smaller unit gives a larger count.
supportHints: Read what a single unit is worth from the first row.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} inspected {{p}}% of the {{total}} {{item}} delivered. How many did they inspect?

solutionReview.headline: A percent of a total is a share of it.

attemptFeedback: The question asks for the inspected part, not the rest.
supportHints: Work out one percent of the delivery first.

documents.prompt: {{part}} {{item}} failed inspection, which was {{p}}% of the batch. How many were in the batch?

solutionReview.headline: Come down to one percent, then up to the whole.
reasoning: One percent is {{hundreds}}, so a hundred percent is {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: The failures are part of the batch, so the batch is larger.
supportHints: What would one percent of the batch be?

documents.prompt: Of {{total}} {{item}} on a {{vehicle}}, {{part}} were damaged. What percent were damaged?

solutionReview.headline: A part becomes a percent by comparing it with the whole.

attemptFeedback: The damaged count is not already a percent.
supportHints: How many hundredths of the load is the damaged part?

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} raised a $\${{price}}$ charge by {{p}}%, then took $\${{cut}}$ off for a trade account. What is the charge now?

solutionReview.headline: The rise goes on the original, then the reduction comes off the result.

attemptFeedback: The rise is added to the charge before the reduction comes off.
supportHints: Handle the two changes in the order the sentence gives them.

documents.prompt: The table records the same order two ways. How many {{item}} are still outstanding?

solutionReview.headline: The two rows are two views of one order.
reasoning: {{filled}} is {{p}} percent, so one percent is {{hundreds}} and the order is {{total}}.

attemptFeedback: The percent in the second row is not a count.
supportHints: The filled row tells you the size of the whole order.

documents.prompt: Four {{shop}} records show shares of one order. Which is the largest share?

solutionReview.headline: Shares only compare once every form matches.
reasoning: Rewrite each record the same way: {{big}}% is {{bigDec}}, and {{midDec}} is {{mid}}%.

attemptFeedback: A record can look larger and still name a smaller share.
supportHints: Put all four into one form before comparing.

documents.prompt: A load of {{total}} {{item}} is split into {{den}} equal parts. How many {{item}} are in {{num}} parts?

solutionReview.headline: Find one part, then take as many as asked.
reasoning: Each part holds {{total}} divided by {{den}}, or {{per}}.

attemptFeedback: The two numbers count parts, not items.
supportHints: Work out the size of a single part first.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} finished {{dec}} of a {{total}}-{{item}} job. How many {{item}} is that?

solutionReview.headline: A decimal share reads as hundredths.
reasoning: {{dec}} of the job is {{p}} percent of it.

attemptFeedback: A decimal share makes the total smaller, not larger.
supportHints: How many hundredths does the decimal name?

documents.prompt: Three clerks recorded the same share of one shipment. Which record does not match the others?

solutionReview.headline: Equivalent records must all name the same share of the whole.
reasoning: The third record uses {{wrongDen}} on the bottom, so it names a different share.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Clerk C’s record is the odd one out.

attemptFeedback: A percent counts hundredths, so the matching fraction is over 100.
supportHints: Two of the records already agree. Find the one that does not.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} records {{num}} of {{den}} {{item}} as sold. Out of 100, that is how many?

solutionReview.headline: Both parts of a fraction scale by the same factor.

attemptFeedback: Both numbers grow by the same factor, not by the same amount.
supportHints: How many times does the bottom number go into 100?

documents.prompt: A {{worker}} earned $\${{pay}}$ for {{hours}} hours. What is the hourly rate?

solutionReview.headline: An hourly rate divides the pay by the hours.
reasoning: The pay covers every hour worked.
{{pay}} shared over {{hours}} hours is {{answer}} an hour.

attemptFeedback: Check which number counts hours and which counts dollars.
supportHints: Decide which quantity is being shared across the other.

documents.prompt: Three {{shop}} offers are listed. What is the lowest price per {{item}}?

solutionReview.headline: Three totals only rank once each is per item.
reasoning: Offer A is {{high}} each, B is {{low}} each and C is {{mid}} each.
The lowest of the three is {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: The cheapest total is not always the cheapest per item.
supportHints: Work out what one item costs under each offer.

documents.prompt: A {{machine}} uses {{ml}} millilitres of oil every {{cycles}} cycles. How much does it use every 10 cycles?

solutionReview.headline: Restating a rate goes through the amount for one.
reasoning: {{ml}} over {{cycles}} cycles is {{unit}} millilitres a cycle.
Ten cycles use ten times that, or {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: The quoted figure covers a different number of cycles.
supportHints: Work out the oil for a single cycle first.

documents.prompt: A supplier charges $\${{total}}$ for {{count}} {{item}}. At the same rate, what do {{want}} {{item}} cost?

solutionReview.headline: Come down to one, then up to the amount ordered.

attemptFeedback: The quoted total covers a different quantity from the one ordered.
supportHints: What does a single one cost?

documents.prompt: A meter read {{r1}} at {{h1}} hours and {{r2}} at {{h2}} hours. How much does it climb each hour?

solutionReview.headline: A per-hour climb needs the change in both columns.
reasoning: The reading rose by {{d_forgotFinalStep}} over {{gap}} hours.

attemptFeedback: The total rise is not the hourly rise.
supportHints: Both the reading and the hours changed. Compare the two changes.

documents.prompt: A {{machine}} produces {{y}} {{item}} in {{x}} hours at a steady rate. How many does it produce each hour?

solutionReview.headline: A steady rate is the output divided by the input.
reasoning: A steady rate means every hour contributes the same amount.

attemptFeedback: Check which column counts hours.
supportHints: One hour is the unit the question wants.

documents.prompt: One row of this steady-rate table is wrong. Which entry does not match the others?

solutionReview.headline: A steady rate gives the same amount per hour in every row.
reasoning: The first two rows both give {{k}} per hour.
At {{x3}} hours a steady rate gives {{y3}}, not {{bad}}.

attemptFeedback: Check each row against the rate the earlier rows set.
supportHints: Work out the per-hour amount from the first two rows.

documents.prompt: A pump moves {{k}} litres a minute. How many litres does it move in {{x}} minutes?

solutionReview.headline: A constant rate multiplies by the time.

attemptFeedback: Pair the per-minute amount with the number of minutes.
supportHints: One minute is worth the stated amount.

documents.prompt: A {{vehicle}} burns {{k}} litres of fuel an hour. How long can it run on {{total}} litres?

solutionReview.headline: A total and a rate give the time.

attemptFeedback: The tank size is shared out at the hourly rate.
supportHints: How many hours worth of fuel does the tank hold?

documents.prompt: Two {{machine}}s ran as logged. How many more {{item}} an hour does the faster one make?

solutionReview.headline: Compare the two rates, not the two totals.
reasoning: Machine A makes {{fast}} an hour and B makes {{slow}}.

attemptFeedback: The machines ran for different lengths of time.
supportHints: Neither total means anything until both are per hour.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} loaded the counts shown over four days. What is the daily average?

solutionReview.headline: An average shares the total evenly across the entries.
reasoning: Shared over four days that is {{answer}} a day.

attemptFeedback: Divide by how many days there are, not by more or fewer.
supportHints: Total the four days, then split the total evenly.

documents.prompt: Four deliveries averaged {{mean}} {{item}}. Three of them carried {{a}}, {{b}} and {{c}}. How many did the fourth carry?

solutionReview.headline: The average fixes the total, and the total fixes the missing entry.
reasoning: Four deliveries averaging {{mean}} carried {{total}} in all.
The first three carried {{d_partialTotal}}, so the fourth carried {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: Work out the total the average implies before looking at the missing one.
supportHints: What must all four add up to?

documents.prompt: Five runs recorded the times shown in minutes. What is the median time?

solutionReview.headline: The median is the middle value once the list is in order.
reasoning: The middle one of five is {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: The middle of the table is not the middle of the ordered list.
supportHints: Put the times in order first.

documents.prompt: Over {{days}} days a {{crew}} logged temperatures from {{low}} to {{high}} degrees. What is the range?

solutionReview.headline: Range is the distance between the highest and lowest.
reasoning: The range measures how far apart the extremes are.

attemptFeedback: The range is a difference, not a total and not the number of days.
supportHints: How far is it from the lowest reading to the highest?

documents.prompt: Three loads averaged {{mean}} {{item}}. A fourth load of {{fourth}} arrives. What is the new average?

solutionReview.headline: A new entry moves the average toward itself, not all the way.
reasoning: With the fourth the total is {{total}} over four loads, or {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: Averaging the old average with the new load is not the same as averaging all four.
supportHints: Rebuild the total, then share it over four loads.

documents.prompt: A {{shop}} scales an order of {{total}} {{item}} by one of these factors. Which gives the largest new order?

solutionReview.headline: A fraction grows a quantity only when its top exceeds its bottom.
reasoning: A factor bigger than 1 grows the order; a factor smaller than 1 shrinks it.
Only $\frac{{{topHeavy}}}{{{den}}}$ has a top larger than its bottom.

attemptFeedback: Multiplying by a fraction below 1 makes the result smaller.
supportHints: Compare the top and bottom of each factor with each other.

documents.prompt: A {{crew}} increased a run of {{total}} {{item}} to {{num}} for every {{den}} it had been. How many {{item}} now?

solutionReview.headline: A factor above one grows the run.
reasoning: {{num}} of those shares is {{answer}}, which is more than it started with.

attemptFeedback: The new run is larger than the old one.
supportHints: Work out one share of the original run first.

documents.prompt: A {{machine}} run of {{total}} {{item}} was cut to {{num}} of every {{den}}. How many {{item}} now?

solutionReview.headline: A factor below one shrinks the run.

attemptFeedback: Cutting a run down leaves fewer than before.
supportHints: How big is a single share of the original run?

documents.prompt: An order of {{total}} {{item}} was changed to {{after}}. How many of every {{den}} were kept?

solutionReview.headline: Work back from the new size to the number of shares kept.

attemptFeedback: The answer counts shares, not items.
supportHints: How big is one share of the original order?

documents.prompt: A run was scaled twice as recorded. How many {{item}} are there at the end?

solutionReview.headline: Each factor applies to what the step before it left.
reasoning: The second step cuts that to {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: Apply the two factors one after the other.
supportHints: The second factor works on the result of the first, not on the start.

documents.prompt: A register opened at $\${{start}}$ and recorded the entries shown. What is the closing balance?

solutionReview.headline: A register runs down the entries in order.
reasoning: Deposits add and withdrawals take away.

attemptFeedback: A withdrawal lowers the balance, and the opening figure is only the starting point.
supportHints: Work down the entries one at a time from the opening balance.

documents.prompt: A register opened at $\${{start}}$, took a deposit of $\${{dep}}$ and one withdrawal, and closed at $\${{end}}$. What was the withdrawal?

solutionReview.headline: Work forward to the point before the unknown entry.
reasoning: After the deposit the balance stood at {{start}} plus {{dep}}.
Falling to {{end}} means {{answer}} was taken out.

attemptFeedback: The deposit lands before the withdrawal, so it counts too.
supportHints: What was the balance just after the deposit?

documents.prompt: An account holding $\${{a}}$ transfers $\${{move}}$ to one holding $\${{b}}$. How much more does the second account now hold than the first?

solutionReview.headline: A transfer moves the amount twice: out of one and into the other.
reasoning: The first account falls to {{newA}} and the second rises to {{newB}}.

attemptFeedback: The gap widens by twice the transfer, because one side loses what the other gains.
supportHints: Both balances change, not just one.

documents.prompt: A register holds $\${{start}}$ with $\${{pending}}$ of payments still to clear. What is the largest whole-dollar withdrawal that keeps the balance at or above zero?

solutionReview.headline: Money already committed is not available.
reasoning: The pending payments are already committed.
Only {{start}} minus {{pending}}, or {{answer}}, is free to withdraw.

attemptFeedback: The pending payments still have to clear.
supportHints: Some of the balance is already spoken for.

documents.prompt: A register logged the four weekly net changes shown. What was the average change per week?

solutionReview.headline: An average change shares the total across the weeks.
reasoning: Shared over four weeks that is {{answer}}.

attemptFeedback: Divide by the number of weeks, not by one more or fewer.
supportHints: Total the four weeks first, including the ones that fell.

documents.prompt: A {{worker}} earning $\${{price}}$ pays {{p}}% income tax in one bracket and {{q}}% in another. How much more tax is paid at the higher rate?

solutionReview.headline: The extra tax comes from the difference in the rates.
reasoning: The two rates differ by {{p}} against {{q}} percent.

attemptFeedback: The question asks for the difference, not either tax on its own.
supportHints: Only the gap between the two rates matters.

documents.prompt: A receipt shows $\${{price}}$ before tax and $\${{total}}$ after. What was the tax rate?
